value: All experiments were ambient laboratory tests, with no complete thermal-vacuum validation.
The ODT ran on an AMD host rather than the lower-clock target MPFS250T, so real-time target confirmation remains outstanding.
The linear ambient model neglects nonlinear radiative terms and empirical smooth bounded trajectories do not replace formal eigenvalue stability analysis.
No statistical contact-resistance characterization was performed.
The model-update implementation uses no regularization, statistical priors, filtering, or repeated fitting windows, and hyperparameter selection was empirical.
One LED path carried nearly all LED workload for much of the orbit, creating possible actuator-loss compliance and wear concerns.
Only one orbit was simulated because early experiments suggested periodic steady state in the first orbit.
Deploy and benchmark the ODT on the target distributed OBC architecture.
Perform thermal-vacuum validation and extend/linearize radiative heat-transfer terms.

The core ODT elements are the Plant Model, the Operation Optimizer, the Model Update routine, the Predicted Disturbance signals, and the Reference.

At each sampling instant, the Plant Model predicts the future thermal state of the payload from the current temperatures, the candidate operation mode, and the predicted external disturbances. The Operation Optimizer uses this model to determine the operation mode that minimizes the temperature differences at the Temperature-Sensitive Components (TSC) while satisfying power and actuator constraints.

The mismatch between measured and predicted states is then processed by the Model Update block to correct the thermal parameters of the Plant Model. In this way, the ODT remains representative even when the thermal behavior deviates from the initial design (see Fig. 5).
